Eurica Cyclic

GeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four circles drawn around a four-sided shape always meet at one point.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or drag the whole shape; focus a corner and use the arrow keys to nudge it. Tick the boxes to show names, the angle hint, or the applet's own choice of the meeting point.
Look for the math

Drag one corner and four circles chase it, yet they still share a single point. The old page asks two things: do the circles always meet, and does that meeting point sit on the line through P and Q? The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra sketch; the archived 28 July 2011 page really embeds CODE="EuricaCyclic" with ShowNames=1, and this port follows that Java applet and its article.

The exact claim

Let P be where the lines AB and CD meet, and Q where BC and AD meet. Draw the circumcircles C(ABQ), C(BCP), C(ADP) and C(CDQ). The page claims all four pass through one point K, and that K is collinear with P and Q. It also says the circles meet even when ABCD is not a cyclic quadrilateral; only the line through P and Q needs the circle. The logic test checks 4,080 drawable four-corner choices in a regular grid, 6,845 cyclic cases in all and 2,000 non-cyclic ones: concurrency holds throughout and collinearity holds on the circle and fails off it.

Why four circles meet

This is the Miquel point of a complete quadrilateral. The circles C(ABQ) and C(BCP) already share B; their other meeting point is K. Because B, A, Q, K lie on one circle and B, P, C, K on another, the angles at K match the angles at A and C, which forces K onto C(ADP) and C(CDQ) as well. The test found no counterexample: the largest distance from the computed K to any of the four circles, measured against the size of the picture, was below 10-7.

Why K lands on PQ

Here the four corners do sit on one circle, so inscribed angles give ∠BCD + ∠BAD = 180°. As P and Q lie on extensions of the sides, ∠BCD + ∠BCP = 180° and ∠BAD + ∠BAQ = 180°. In the two circles through K, ∠BCP + ∠BKP = 180° and ∠BAQ + ∠BKQ = 180°. Adding these with the first pair gives

∠BKP + ∠BKQ = 180°,

which is exactly what it means for P, K and Q to lie on one straight line. Every one of the 6,845 cyclic cases tested had this sum, to within a ten-millionth of the picture's size.

One shortcut in the Java applet

Two circles meet in two points: B and K. The applet's Other() method keeps the first one unless it is within one unit of P, so it often shows B where the page's K should be: in 2,517 of the 4,080 grid cases. This port follows the page's claim and draws the point that really lies on all four circles. Tick "Applet's K" to see a red ring at the Java applet's raw choice when it differs. Two more guards from the bytecode remain faithful: a side pair whose line determinant is below one has no intersection drawn, and two circles whose centres are within a unit of each other fall back to their centre.

Try dragging one corner far off the grey circle: the four circles still meet, but the line through P and Q misses K. Press Reset to put everything back.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
